1:
The chapter opens on the notorious tangle of its own date, and the witnesses divide sharply over how "the six and thirtieth year" can be squared with a king of Israel who, by the older record, had been dead a decade. The reformed John Gill states the difficulty plainly — Baasha reigned but twenty-four years, beginning in Asa’s third, so that he must have died nearly ten years before this thirty-sixth year — and, rather than solve it here, refers the reader to his fuller treatment at 1 Kings 15:16, where the same events are related.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry confesses himself "quite at a loss." Baasha died in the twenty-sixth year of Asa, as 1 Kings 16:8 records; how then could he build Ramah in Asa’s thirty-sixth, when his house was already cut off and Omri on the throne? Henry rehearses the common answer — that the reckoning runs not from Asa’s accession but from the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam, so coinciding with the sixteenth of his reign — yet finds it broken by 2 Chronicles 15:19, which then falls in Asa’s own fifteenth year, the very year of the covenant at 2 Chronicles 15:10. He inclines instead to Josephus, who set the war in Asa’s twenty-sixth year, and to the supposition of a transcriber’s error both here and at that earlier notice.

The wesleyan-arminian voices take the reckoning Henry doubted. Adam Clarke, following Usher, reads "the six and thirtieth year" as counted from the division of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. John Wesley spells out the arithmetic: Rehoboam’s seventeen years, Abijah’s three, and Asa’s fifteen make thirty-five, the figure named at 2 Chronicles 15:19, so that in the next year Baasha went to war.

The other grammatical-historical witness will have none of it. Charles Ellicott judges the statements simply irreconcilable and prefers the surgeon’s remedy: the text is unsound, "thirty-six" a scribal substitution for sixteen or twenty-six, and "thirty-five" at 2 Chronicles 15:19 a like mistake for fifteen or twenty-five. The idea of the ancient commentators that the phrase means the thirty-sixth year of the kingdom of Judah he calls flatly "absurd," since the Hebrew idiom always denotes a king’s reign. The witnesses thus leave the date contested: reckoned from the schism, as Clarke and Wesley hold, or mended by emendation, as Ellicott and, leaning, Henry prefer, while Gill defers the whole knot to his notes on Kings.
2:
Asa’s embassy to Damascus is bought with the treasures of the temple, and the witnesses read the transaction both as a piece of textual craft and as a spiritual scandal. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch observe that the whole account of this war, through v.6, agrees almost word for word with 1 Kings 15:17 and the verses following, the chronicler having "mentioned only the main things"; the fuller comment, they note, belongs to the exposition of the older book.

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Charles Ellicott marks the small but telling changes. The verse is abridged from 1 Kings 15:18, and its differences are characteristic. Where Kings says Asa took "all the silver and the gold that were left in the treasures of the house of the LORD," the chronicler has purposely weakened the statement, softening the plunder; he has dropped the pedigree of Benhadad — son of Tabrimmon, son of Hezion — and written the later Aramaizing form Darmeseq for Damascus. The philology, in Ellicott’s hands, betrays a compiler handling his source with a careful and reverent hand.

But it is the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry who presses what the money meant. To take silver and gold out of the house of the LORD for such a purpose, he says, was a great aggravation of the sin: "Must the temple be plundered to serve his carnal politics?" Asa had far better have brought gifts and offerings, with prayers and supplications, into that same house, that he might have engaged God on his side and made him his friend; then he would not have needed to be at this expense to make Benhadad his friend. The very treasury that should have furnished a thank-offering is rifled to hire a heathen ally — the act of a king who trusts an arm of flesh more than the God whose house he robs.

The witnesses do not finally divide; they light the verse from two sides. Keil and Ellicott fix the text — its near-identity with the older record, its deliberate abridgements, its softened phrasing and later spelling — while Henry weighs the deed on the scales of the sanctuary and finds it wanting. Together they show a transaction that was at once shrewd statecraft and quiet apostasy: the treasures dedicated to God spent to purchase the friendship of Syria, so that the help Asa should have sought at the altar he went out to buy at Damascus. It is upon this misplaced confidence that the prophet Hanani will presently fasten his rebuke.
3:
The terms Asa proposes to Benhadad — a league renewed, a bribe paid, an old alliance broken — draw the witnesses to weigh the morality of the whole diplomacy. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads "there is a league" as the offer of a treaty offensive and defensive between the two kings. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the sense of the word — berith, a covenant — and notes that the verse stands almost exactly as 1 Kings 15:19, omitting only "a present" before "silver and gold" and making two or three minute verbal changes, the "depart" of the common version reading in the older text rather "go up."

The heavier weight falls from the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, who finds Asa faulty at several points in this single overture. First, he did not do well to make a league with Benhadad, a heathen king, and to value himself so much upon it; had he relied more on his own covenant, and his father’s, with God, he would not have boasted so of his league, and his father’s, with the royal house of Syria. Second, a due regard to the honour of Israel would have found some other expedient to divert Baasha than calling in a foreign force and inviting into the land a common enemy who might one day be a plague to Judah too. Third — and sharpest — it was a sin in Benhadad to break his league with Baasha upon no provocation, merely for a bribe; and if so, it was a sin in Asa to move him to it, and to hire him to do it. "The public faith of kings and kingdoms," Henry insists, "must not be made so cheap a thing."

So the witnesses set a plain transaction against a searching conscience. Clarke and Ellicott establish what the verse says — a defensive alliance sealed with gold, borrowed almost verbatim from the older narrative — while Henry exposes what it costs: a covenant with an idolater prized above the covenant with God, a neighbouring nation embroiled for Judah’s convenience, and a solemn treaty dissolved for money at Judah’s instigation. The very language of "thy father and my father" betrays where Asa’s confidence now rests — not in the God who had delivered him from a million Ethiopians, but in the hereditary goodwill of Damascus. Henry’s threefold indictment prepares the ground for Hanani’s charge, that in trusting Syria the king had distrusted the LORD.
4:
Benhadad takes the bribe and turns his captains loose on the northern towns, and the witnesses attend both to the places named and to the blood the bargain spilt. The two grammatical-historical voices work at the geography and the odd form of one name. Keil and Delitzsch identify Abel-maim, "Abel in the water," as only another name for the Abel-Beth-Maachah of the older account, pointing back to 2 Samuel 20:14; and they note that the Chronicle’s "store cities of Naphtali" stands where Kings has "all Cinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali," judging the chronicler’s phrase most probably a paraphrase of the unusual reading before him.

Charles Ellicott presses the same points with his lexicon open. Abel-maim, he says, is nowhere else so called, and the name is perhaps an early mistake for Abel-Beth-Maachah. The "store cities" — miskenoth, the magazines of 2 Chronicles 8:4 — answer to the Cinneroth of 1 Kings 15:20, a town of Naphtali named at Joshua 19:35 that gave its name to the Sea of Cinneroth at Joshua 12:3; probably the fertile district west of the lake bore the name too, and this was the country Benhadad’s army laid waste. The present reading, he allows, may be a textual corruption or a deliberate paraphrase — he prefers the latter — of what stood in the older record.

Against this careful map the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets a moral reckoning. It was well, he says, if Asa had not to answer for all the mischief that the army of Benhadad did unjustly to the cities of Israel — all the blood they shed and all the spoil they made. Perhaps Asa never intended the matter to be carried so far; but those who draw others into sin know not what they do, nor where it will end, "for the beginning of sin is as the letting forth of water." The king who hired a heathen sword to divert Baasha becomes, in Henry’s reading, a partner in every cruelty that sword inflicted.

The witnesses do not divide; they simply divide the task. Keil and Ellicott settle the towns on the land and trace the strange name and the store-cities back through the older record; Henry counts the human cost of Asa’s policy. Between them the verse becomes more than a raid: it is the visible fruit of a bribe, a swathe of Naphtali plundered so that Judah might have peace, and a burden of guilt that Henry lays, with the spoilers, at the door of the king who paid them.
5:
Baasha’s response to the raid is told in a single clause — he abandons the fortress he was raising and lets the work fall — and the witnesses, few here, read in it both a textual curiosity and the success of Asa’s stratagem. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes his attention on the wording. "And let his work cease" stands where the older account at 1 Kings 15:21 reads "and dwelt in Tirzah"; the partial likeness of the Hebrew, he observes, is obvious. Kings appears to preserve the correct text, and the chronicler’s tautologous phrase — for "left off building" and "let his work cease" say nearly the same thing twice — Ellicott ascribes to a fault in the writer’s manuscript, a slip of copying rather than a change of sense.

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch had already noted that the whole account of this war agrees almost literally with the parallel in the older history, so that the substance is not in doubt however the one clause be read; and the reformed John Gill, treating the verse as matter already related, contents himself with referring the reader to the fuller narrative rather than repeating it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies the strategy the bare verse assumes. Benhadad’s onslaught in the north gave Baasha a powerful diversion, obliging him to leave off building Ramah and to betake himself instead to the defence of his own country northward, now overrun by the Syrian captains. Ramah, the frontier stronghold with which Baasha had meant to blockade Judah and stop the passage to and from Asa’s kingdom, is suddenly forsaken; the king of Israel, threatened at home, cannot afford to press his works against Judah abroad. Asa’s gold has done precisely what his prayers might have done more honourably — cleared his border of the encroaching fortress.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott secures the letter of the verse and marks the manuscript flaw that doubled its verb; Keil and Gill confirm its agreement with the received history; Henry unfolds the military logic that makes the clause intelligible. Between them they show the hinge of the whole episode turning: the moment Baasha hears of the invasion, his grand design against Judah collapses, and the abandoned stones of Ramah lie ready for another hand to carry off. The stratagem has worked, and worked completely — a fact that will make Hanani’s rebuke the harder to bear, for the very success of the sin is what tempts a man to justify it.
6:
The episode ends with Asa turning his enemy’s building-materials to his own use, and the witnesses follow both the levy that gathered the stones and the two forts they raised. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads "took all Judah" as the general muster of the people for the work, referring back to the parallel at 1 Kings 15:22. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the comparison: where the older record says pointedly that "the king Asa called together all Judah; none was exempted," the chronicler has modified an obscure sentence into a smoother one. The rest of the verse coincides with Kings, save that the older text names the first fort "Geba of Benjamin"; and for the second, Mizpah, Ellicott recalls that Jeremiah 41:9 and the verse following mention the great cistern Asa made there "for fear of Baasha king of Israel," a work of the same defensive campaign.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the completeness of Asa’s advantage. Baasha’s forced retreat gave the king of Judah an opportunity not only to demolish the fortifications at Ramah but to seize the very materials and convert them to his own use. The stones and timber quarried and hewn to blockade Judah are carried off to build Judah’s own defences; the fortress meant to hem Asa in becomes the strengthening of his frontier. What Baasha had gathered for aggression, Asa turns to protection — Geba and Mizpah rising from the wreck of Ramah.

The reformed John Gill, who had treated the whole passage as matter already told, is content to send the reader to the older narrative for the details rather than expound them afresh.

The witnesses do not divide. Clarke and Gill anchor the verse in its parallel; Ellicott mends the chronicler’s smoothed-over sentence, restores the "of Benjamin" that Kings attaches to Geba, and ties Mizpah to Jeremiah’s later notice of its cistern; Henry reads the whole as the visible profit of the stratagem. Between them the verse rounds off the war on a note of worldly success — the border cleared, the enemy’s works dismantled, two strongholds built from the spoil. Yet the reader who has heard Henry’s earlier misgivings feels the irony the chronicler is preparing: every stone of this triumph was won by a bribe drawn from the temple, and the more complete the success, the sharper will be the word of the seer who comes, in the next verse, to call it folly. The prosperity of the deed is real; its righteousness is precisely what Hanani will deny.
7:
At the height of his success the seer arrives with a rebuke, and the witnesses gather in force around Hanani and his charge. The reformed John Gill notes simply that the prophet was sent by God to reprove the king. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch place him: Hanani is met with only here, but Jehu the son of Hanani, who denounced Baasha’s house at 1 Kings 16:1 and reappeared under Jehoshaphat at 2 Chronicles 19:2, was without doubt his son. The gist of the charge, they explain with Bertheau, is that had Asa relied on God he would have conquered not only Baasha’s army but the host of Damascus too, which now, through his league, had slipped from his grasp.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, weighs the title and the theology. "The seer," ha-roeh, is the old word explained at 1 Samuel 9:9, and its use points to an ancient source peculiar to the chronicler. Hanani’s words, he urges, are in perfect accord with the teaching of the greater prophets — with Isaiah’s scorn of those who trust in the arm of Egypt at Isaiah 31:1 and Jeremiah’s curse on him that maketh flesh his arm at Jeremiah 17:5 — a harmony that favours their authenticity. Asa had feared that Benhadad would join Baasha against him and bribed him at the temple’s expense; the politic act secured its object, but from the prophetic view such success was no better than loss, for it robbed Asa of an assured triumph over the combined forces of Israel and Syria.

On that lost victory the wesleyan-arminian voices concur. Adam Clarke reads "escaped out of thine hand" as meaning that divine providence had intended to give Asa a grand victory over the Syrians, Israel’s inveterate enemies, and that his ill-judged alliance thwarted the purpose, so the Syrians escaped. John Wesley makes the same point with an eye to the future: Benhadad is reserved to be a scourge to Asa’s kingdom and posterity, whereas had he joined with Baasha, Asa should have overthrown them both and prevented all the mischief that monarch would yet do.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a doctrine of distrust. The prophet’s charge, he says, fastens on the king’s greatest fault — relying on the king of Syria and not on the LORD his God. God is much displeased when he is distrusted and when an arm of flesh is relied on more than his power and goodness; by putting our confidence in him we give him honour, and therefore he counts himself affronted when that honour is given to another. Asa thought that God’s being on his side would not serve unless he had Benhadad on it too. The witnesses do not divide: Gill and Ellicott establish the prophet and his pedigree; Keil, Clarke, and Wesley reckon the victory his sin forfeited; Henry names the sin itself, a heart that could not trust the God it had so often proved.
8:
The seer clinches his charge with an appeal to memory — the vast army of Zerah that God had already delivered into Asa’s hand — and the witnesses expound both the old victory and the argument it carries. The reformed John Gill recalls the scale of that former host: the Ethiopians and the Lubim were no less than a million men with three hundred chariots, the Lubim being the Libyans who dwelt in Africa near Egypt, whom an Arabic writer takes for the Nubians. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that the Lubim were the Libyans of Africa, or a kindred people descended from them and now seated in some part of Arabia.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the verse an exact confirmation of the one before. Cushites and Libyans were banded together in Zerah’s great army just as Syrians and Israelites might have united to assail Judah, yet the victory had fallen to Asa, as the narrative of the earlier deliverance at 2 Chronicles 14:9 and the verses following records; and since Cushites and Libyans were likewise among Shishak’s forces at 2 Chronicles 12:3, Zerah was clearly master of Egypt. He notes that the Hebrew here is unmistakably the chronicler’s own, and that neither the Libyan contingent nor the horsemen were named in the earlier account — a sign that the writer drew on fuller sources than he had there used.

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the ground of the great sentence to follow: Jahve, whose eyes run over all the earth, uses every opportunity to succour those who are piously devoted to him — the verb, they note, being the "help mightily" of 1 Chronicles 11:10. The one who relied on God against a million was chidden for hiring a Syrian against Baasha.

That contrast is the whole of the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry’s reading. Asa, he says, acted against his own experience: he of all men had no reason to distrust God, who had made him triumph over so threatening an enemy precisely because he relied on the LORD. "Were not the Ethiopians and the Lubim a huge host, enough to swallow up a kingdom? And yet, because thou didst rely on the Lord, he delivered them into thy hand; and was not he sufficient to help thee against Baasha?" The many experiences we have had of God’s goodness, Henry concludes, do but aggravate our distrust of him — for he who has helped us in six troubles is not to be suspected in the seventh. The witnesses do not divide: Gill and Wesley identify the peoples and their numbers; Ellicott ties the verse to the earlier victory and marks the chronicler’s fuller sources; Keil hears in it the opening of the next verse’s promise; Henry drives home the folly of distrusting a God so often proved.
9:
The heart of Hanani’s reproof is a great sentence on providence, and the witnesses linger over the sweep of the divine gaze and the sting of its application. The reformed John Gill takes the "eyes of the LORD" for both his omniscience, which is everywhere, and the eyes of his mercy and care, which are here and there and in every place throughout the whole world at once. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the Hebrew more pointedly — "For Jehovah, his eyes run to and fro" — and notes that the very phrase recurs in the vision of Zechariah 4:10 and lies behind the roaming survey of Job 1:7. To "show himself strong" for the perfect-hearted is a construction dear to the chronicler, who supplies fifteen of the twenty-seven times the verb occurs in Scripture; and "thou hast done foolishly" he reads as "thou hast shown thyself foolish," the word of David’s own confession at 2 Samuel 24:10. The threatened "wars," set against the peace Asa had enjoyed, he takes as a warning that peace bought by worldly policy will not last — a lesson verified again in Judah’s later history, as when Ahaz met disaster at 2 Chronicles 28:20 and the verse following.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fasten on the "foolishly" and the "perfect heart." John Wesley calls it a foolish thing to lean on a broken reed when we have the rock of ages to rely upon, and reads "perfect" as upright and sincere — "as thine is not," for though Asa was sincere in the general course of his life, in this particular his heart did not perfectly cleave to God. Adam Clarke marks the fulfilment of the threat: Asa did indeed have wars during the rest of his reign, as 1 Kings 15:32 records.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the doctrine at length. Asa, he says, acted against his very knowledge of God and his providence. The eye of Providence is quick-sighted — it runs; it is intent — it runs to and fro; it reaches far — through the whole earth, no corner of which is hidden from it. From this Henry gathers three truths: that God governs the world in infinite wisdom, so that the creatures and all their actions are continually under his eye; that he governs it for the good of his people, in pursuance of the counsels of his love; and that those whose hearts are upright with him may therefore be sure of his protection. A practical disbelief of this, Henry adds, lies at the bottom of all our departures from God — Asa could not trust him, and therefore made court to Benhadad; and now, for his folly, he must expect no peace but the constant alarms of war. The witnesses do not divide; together they leave Asa condemned out of the very providence that had so often saved him.
10:
The rebuke that should have humbled the king only enrages him, and the witnesses read his violence as the terrible unravelling of a good man. The reformed John Gill sees in Asa’s wrath at so faithful a reproof yet another instance of his sin and folly. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry is more astonished still: "Is this Asa?" — the king whose heart was perfect with the LORD all his days, now in a rage with a prophet, impatient of reproof, unable to bear being told of his fault. Let him that thinks he stands, Henry warns, take heed lest he fall. Asa proceeds to two outrages: he commits the prophet to jail, as a malefactor, in the stocks; and, going further, he oppresses some of the people — probably those who owned the prophet in his sufferings. He that abused his power to persecute God’s messenger was left to himself to abuse it further in crushing his own subjects; and Henry lays down the grim rule that most persecutors have been tyrants.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the instrument and the fury. Keil and Delitzsch render "prison house" as the stock-house, from mahpecheth, a twisting engine of torture by which the body was forced into an unnatural posture, hands and feet bent together, the same word that meets us at Jeremiah 20:2 and Jeremiah 29:26 and behind the fastening of Paul’s feet at Acts 16:24. Hanani’s speech, and still more the king’s harsh handling of him, they observe, bred great discontent among the people, so that Asa felt compelled to crush the murmurers. Charles Ellicott confirms the sense of the stocks against the milder "prison" of the Syriac and Septuagint, compares Ahab’s like treatment of Micaiah at 1 Kings 22:26 and the verse following, and reads the oppression as the violent suppression of those who had sympathised with the seer, the same verb of crushing that meets us at 1 Samuel 12:3.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke traces the moral descent. Instead of humbling himself and deprecating the displeasure of the LORD, Asa persecuted his messenger; and having laid violent hands on the prophet, he seems to have had his heart hardened through the deceitfulness of sin, so that he began to oppress the people too, whether by unjust imprisonments or by excessive taxations.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Henry lament the fall of a good king into rage and cruelty; Keil and Ellicott expose the very engine of torture and the violence done to the people; Clarke charts the hardening that carried Asa from persecuting one prophet to oppressing many subjects. Between them they show how swiftly a heart that will not bear reproof passes from folly into tyranny — the same king who had leaned on Damascus now stopping the mouth that told him so, and putting into the stocks the man God had sent to save him.
11:
The standing closing-formula now falls upon Asa’s reign — his acts "first and last" consigned to the royal annals — and the witnesses, brief here, attend to the record it invokes and the source it names. The reformed John Gill, treating the notice as matter already handled, refers the reader to his comment on the parallel rather than expounding it afresh. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark it as the formal close of the reign, answering to the like notice in the older history at 1 Kings 15:23 and the verse following, and refer for the nature of "the book of the kings of Judah and Israel" to their general Introduction; the title, they observe, embraces both kingdoms, though Asa reigned over Judah alone.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, glosses "the acts of Asa" as his history, and observes something the cross-reference quietly confirms. The corresponding verse of the older book, in summing up Asa’s reign, mentions his "might" or prowess and "the cities that he built"; and those two notices, Ellicott points out, corroborate the fuller account the chronicler has given in 2 Chronicles 14:6 and the verses about it of the king’s defensive measures and of the great invasion of Zerah — matter the older record passes over almost in silence. The compiler, that is, is not inventing where he expands, but drawing on ampler sources whose existence the very formula of Kings attests.

The witnesses do not divide, and the seemingly bare verse repays their attention. The formula that appears to do no more than defer to the state chronicles in fact marks the chronicler’s method: he writes selectively, pressing on to the matter that serves his purpose — here the sin and sickness and death of a king who began well and ended badly — while leaving the full civil and military record to the common annals he names. Gill sends the reader to the older book; Keil fixes the notice as the reign’s formal close; Ellicott shows how the "might" and "cities" of the older summary vouch for the chronicler’s own narrative of Asa’s building and his war. Between them they let the verse do its proper work, turning the reader from the outward acts of the reign, sufficiently recorded elsewhere, toward the inward and spiritual reckoning that the next verses will complete — the tale not of what Asa built or conquered, but of how a heart once perfect toward God came, in its last years, to seek help everywhere but from him.
12:
Two years before his death Asa is struck in the feet, and the witnesses read both the disease and his response to it as the fitting close of his decline. The reformed John Gill takes the malady for the gout and hears in it a just retaliation: the king who had put the prophet’s feet in the stocks is now himself afflicted in his feet. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the same poetic justice — "he had put the prophet in the stocks, and now God put him in the stocks; so his punishment answered his sin." Yet the disease, Henry insists, was not the fault; the fault was that in his disease, instead of seeking to the LORD for relief, Asa sought to the physicians. To use physicians was his duty; but to trust in them, and to expect from them what was to be had from God only, was his sin and folly.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses say the same in their own key. John Wesley grants that making use of physicians was Asa’s duty, but his trusting in their skill and faithfulness, without humbling himself before God, was his sin: the help of every creature must be used with an eye to the Creator, in dependence on him who makes every creature to us what it is. Adam Clarke, citing the Targum, glosses that Asa "did not seek discipline from the face of the LORD, but from the physicians," and draws the lesson that we should make supplication in our afflictions, looking to be healed when God finds us duly humbled.

Whether these were ordinary healers, however, the witnesses are not agreed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the verb "sought" is here construed as it is for seeking an oracle or consulting idols at 1 Samuel 28:7 and 2 Kings 1:2, so that what is censured is not the mere consulting of physicians but the godless manner of Asa’s trust in them. Charles Ellicott goes further: like Ahaziah, Asa neglected to consult Jehovah through his priests and preferred the "healers" of his day, whose art probably consisted in magical appliances — amulets, charms, and exorcisms — after the fashion of Babylon and Assyria. Gill and Henry record the same suspicion, that "some think" these physicians were strangers to the commonwealth of Israel, a sort of conjurers, as if there were no God in Israel to consult.

So a real shade of difference runs through the agreement. All the witnesses hold that the sin lay in misplaced confidence, not in medicine; but where Wesley, Clarke, and Henry picture lawful physicians wrongly trusted, Keil and Ellicott — and the "some" Gill and Henry mention — suspect a resort to heathen and magical practitioners, an idolatry of the sickbed. Ellicott adds the philologist’s marks: the disease’s severity, "exceeding great," is the chronicler’s own added phrase, as at 1 Chronicles 22:5, and the older account at 1 Kings 15:23 leaves the malady, like these witnesses, without a name.
13:
The death-notice is brief and formulaic, and the witnesses, few here, weigh chiefly the reckoning of the years and the manner in which the chronicler tells it. The reformed John Gill glosses the settled idiom simply: Asa "slept with his fathers," that is, he died, going the common way of all his ancestors. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the figure "one and fortieth year," noting that the older record at 1 Kings 15:24 gives no such number at this point but passes straight to the usual formula — "buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his stead" — while the total length of the reign, forty-one years, is fixed earlier at 1 Kings 15:10. The chronicler, that is, has carried the regnal figure down to the death-notice itself.

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch read the verse together with the burial that follows, and remark that the Chronicle gives a fuller and more exact account of Asa’s interment than the older history: he was laid not in the common tomb of the kings but in a sepulchre he had prepared for himself in the city of David. That difference — the bare notice of the older book against the circumstantial description of the Chronicle — the two witnesses take as characteristic of the chronicler’s fuller sources and his interest in the honours paid to the ancient kings of Judah.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the sense of the idiom; Ellicott secures the chronology against the parallel; Keil marks the greater fulness of the Chronicle’s account. Between them the verse serves as the quiet turning from the story of Asa’s sin and sickness to the record of his burial: the reign that opened in such zeal and victory, and darkened in its last years into distrust, persecution, and a disease unhealed for want of seeking God, closes at length in the ordinary rest of kings. Asa sleeps with his fathers after one and forty years upon the throne; and the chronicler, having told without flattery how the good king fell, will yet allow him, in the verse that follows, an honourable and even magnificent grave. The idiom of "sleeping with his fathers" grants him the outward dignity of continuity with the house of David, whatever the failings of his latter days — a dignity the next verse will render in spices and fire.
14:
Asa’s funeral closes the chapter in spices and fire, and the witnesses gather around the splendour of the grave, dividing gently over what the burning was and what it meant. The reformed John Gill notes the tomb itself — "his own sepulchres," a vault the king had made with several cells to receive separate bodies, himself and his family. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds that these particulars are the chronicler’s own addition; the plural marks a family tomb of many chambers, not the ordinary royal graves, and "which he had made" means digged or hewn from the rock, so that Asa, like the Pharaohs, prepared his own last resting-place, as the like phrase implies at Isaiah 22:16. The "sweet odours" are the besamim of 2 Chronicles 9:1, the "divers kinds" a rare Aramaic word found besides only at Psalms 144:13, and the "apothecaries’ art" the compounding of ointment described at Exodus 30:25.

On the "very great burning" the witnesses part company. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke thinks it very likely that the body of Asa was itself burnt, the "bed" being a funeral pyre heaped with spices and odoriferous woods, and he adorns the note with Virgil’s account of the burning of Misenus; though he grants that some hold only the aromatics were consumed, in the king’s honour, and not the body. Ellicott, rendering "and they made" literally as "and they burned," takes it rather of the burning of aromatic woods and spices, the usual honour at the obsequies of kings, as at 2 Chronicles 21:19 and Jeremiah 34:5; and John Wesley agrees that the burning was of precious spices, testifying the people’s respect to Asa notwithstanding his miscarriages. So the one witness leans to a true cremation, the others to a burning of spices about the body — a difference the obscure verse leaves open.

A second question is whether the lavish rites were vanity or honour. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reports that some read the funeral pomp as an instance of the king’s own vanity, that he would be buried like the Gentiles, since he "digged the sepulchre for himself"; but Henry is loth to think it, and willing rather to believe the magnificence an expression of the great respect his people retained for him, notwithstanding the failings of his latter days. "Let their faults be buried in their graves," he urges, "while their services are remembered over their graves; the memory of the just is blessed." Ellicott takes exactly the same side against Zöckler, denying any ground for supposing the chronicler blames the splendour as though it were the burial of an Egyptian Pharaoh; the writer who so delighted to dwell on the glory of Solomon plainly meant the extraordinary store of spices to mark Asa’s distinction and his subjects’ esteem.

The witnesses do not, in the end, divide over the verse’s temper. Gill and Ellicott fix the tomb and the spices; Clarke, Ellicott, and Wesley weigh the burning; Henry and Ellicott defend the honour of the rite against those who would read it as pride. Between them they lay the flawed but faithful king to rest with dignity — his sins told without flattery, his grave adorned without reproach — so that the chapter which began with his folly ends with his people’s love, and the memory of a reign that, for all its late darkness, was remembered as the reign of a just man.
